Cities in California.Los Angeles: Its full original name was El Pueblo de Nuestra Senora la Reina de los Angeles, and its river is mostly a concrete channel.
Cities in California.San Francisco: The Golden Gate Bridge is painted 'international orange', a color chosen so it stands out in the city's fog.
Cities in California.San Diego: Home to the San Diego Zoo and the nation's biggest Navy fleet presence, it was where Europeans first landed in California in 1542.
Cities in California.Sacramento: The state capital grew from the 1849 Gold Rush and has more trees per capita than almost any big US city, earning the nickname City of Trees.
Cities in California.San Jose: The heart of Silicon Valley and California's third-largest city, it was the state's first civic settlement, founded in 1777.
Cities in California.Oakland: Across the bay from San Francisco, this port city gave the world the Black Panther Party and is home to one of the busiest container ports on the West Coast.
Cities in California.Fresno: In the middle of the Central Valley, this city anchors one of the world's richest farming counties, famous for raisins and almonds.
Cities in California.Palo Alto: Its name means tall stick in Spanish, after a redwood landmark still standing; Stanford University and many tech giants started here.
Cities in California.Malibu: The name comes from a Chumash village, Humaliwo, meaning 'the surf sounds loudly'; this strip is known for celebrity homes and long beaches.
Cities in California.Pasadena: Every New Year's Day the Rose Parade rolls through here, a tradition dating to 1890, and the Rose Bowl is nearby.
Cities in California.Santa Barbara: Its red-tile Spanish Colonial Revival look was a deliberate rebuild after a 1925 earthquake, giving it the nickname American Riviera.
Cities in California.Anaheim: Disneyland opened here in 1955 on former orange groves, and the name blends the Santa Ana River with the German 'heim', meaning home.
Cities in California.Las Vegas: Trap: this is Nevada's neon city, not California's, even though many Californians drive the roughly 270 miles to get there.
Cities in California.Reno: Trap: Nevada's 'Biggest Little City' sits on California's border near Lake Tahoe, yet it belongs to the Silver State.
Cities in California.Phoenix: Trap: Arizona's capital, named for the mythical bird because it rose on the ruins of an ancient Hohokam canal system.
Cities in California.Portland: Trap: Oregon's city of roses is north of the state line, and its name came from a coin toss between two founders.
Cities in California.Seattle: Trap: this Washington city is named after Chief Si'ahl of the Duwamish and Suquamish peoples, and it lies far north of California.
Cities in California.Tucson: Trap: southern Arizona's desert city, whose name comes from an O'odham word for the dark base of a nearby mountain.
Cities in California.Salt Lake City: Trap: Utah's capital, founded by Mormon pioneers in 1847, and it sits beside a lake saltier than the ocean.
Cities in California.Santa Fe: Trap: it sounds Californian, but this is New Mexico's capital and the oldest US state capital, around 1610.
Cities in California.Tijuana: Trap: the Mexican city sits right at California's southern border, but it is in Baja California, Mexico.
Cities in California.Boise: Trap: Idaho's capital, whose name is said to come from the French les bois, 'the woods', which early trappers shouted on seeing its river trees.
Cities in California.San Antonio: Trap: it has a Californian ring, but this is Texas, where the Alamo mission stands in the city center.
Cities in California.Albuquerque: Trap: New Mexico's city hosts the world's largest hot-air balloon festival every October, far inland from California.

Real countries (not fictional ones).Liechtenstein: A tiny Alpine principality of about 38,000 people, and it is one of just two doubly landlocked countries.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Kiribati: Pronounced 'KEER-ih-bahss', its Gilbert Islands spread over millions of square kilometers across the Pacific.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Tuvalu: One of the smallest nations, its land is highly threatened by rising seas, and its .tv domain suffix is sold to TV companies.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Djibouti: A small country at the Horn of Africa that hosts military bases of the US, France, and China, and has one of the saltiest lakes on Earth, Lake Assal.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Eswatini: It changed its name from Swaziland in 2018, and it is one of Africa's few remaining absolute monarchies.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Burkina Faso: Its name means land of upright people, and it replaced Upper Volta in 1984.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Comoros: A volcanic island nation off Africa, and it is a major source of ylang-ylang for perfume.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Bhutan: The Himalayan kingdom keeps a careful limit on tourism and has no traffic lights in its capital.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Palau: Its Rock Islands and jellyfish lake draw divers, and it was the first country to ban sunscreens that harm coral.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Nauru: Its island is only about 21 square kilometers, making it the third-smallest country by area.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Vanuatu: This island nation is where bungee jumping began, from land diving on Pentecost Island.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Kyrgyzstan: A mountainous Central Asian country, where about 90 percent of the land sits above 1,500 meters.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Wakanda: Trap: the hidden African nation from Marvel's Black Panther comics, first appearing in 1966, is fictional.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Genovia: Trap: the small European principality ruled by Amelia Thermopolis in The Princess Diaries is invented.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Latveria: Trap: Doctor Doom's Marvel kingdom, which sounds like Latvia, is fictional.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Zubrowka: Trap: the alpine country in The Grand Budapest Hotel is fictional, and its name came from a Polish vodka.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Freedonia: Trap: the country run by Groucho Marx in Duck Soup, 1933, is made up.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Sokovia: Trap: the Eastern European country in Marvel's Avengers: Age of Ultron is fictional.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Ruritania: Trap: the fictional kingdom of The Prisoner of Zenda, 1894, gave its name to a whole genre of romances.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Elbonia: Trap: the mud-filled country in the Dilbert comic strip is fictional.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Tatarstan: Trap: it is a real republic, but it is part of Russia, not an independent country, with its capital in Kazan.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Atlantis: Trap: the lost island described by Plato in about 360 BC as an allegory, not a real nation.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Borduria: Trap: the dictatorship fighting Syldavia in Tintin comics is fictional.
Real countries (not fictional ones).Narnia: Trap: C.S. Lewis's magical land reached through a wardrobe is fictional.

Counties of England.Kent: Nicknamed the Garden of England for its orchards and hop fields, it also holds the White Cliffs of Dover.
Counties of England.Essex: Colchester, in Essex, was the first Roman capital of Britain and is often called Britain's oldest recorded town.
Counties of England.Devon: It is the only English county with coastlines on two different seas, the English Channel and the Bristol Channel.
Counties of England.Cornwall: Its flag, a white cross on black, honours St Piran, patron saint of tin miners, who is said to have discovered tin.
Counties of England.Norfolk: The Broads look natural but were dug by hand: they are flooded medieval peat pits, now a network of waterways.
Counties of England.Suffolk: At Sutton Hoo, archaeologists found an Anglo-Saxon royal ship burial packed with treasure, in a grave mound near the coast.
Counties of England.Surrey: Runnymede, where King John sealed Magna Carta in 1215, lies in this county just outside London.
Counties of England.Dorset: The Jurassic Coast is a World Heritage fossil trail, where Mary Anning found her famous ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons.
Counties of England.Somerset: Cheddar Gorge gave the world cheddar cheese, which was originally matured in the gorge's caves.
Counties of England.Cumbria: It holds England's highest mountain, Scafell Pike, and deepest lake, Wastwater, both in the Lake District.
Counties of England.Lancashire: Its red rose was the badge of the House of Lancaster in the Wars of the Roses, and still appears on its flag.
Counties of England.Cheshire: It lent its name to the grinning Cheshire Cat in Alice in Wonderland, as well as to a crumbly cheese.
Counties of England.Shropshire: Ironbridge Gorge here has the world's first major iron bridge, finished in 1779 and a symbol of the Industrial Revolution.
Counties of England.Fife: A Scottish kingdom-turned-region, home to St Andrews, where golf has been played for centuries.
Counties of England.Powys: It is a Welsh county and the largest in Wales by area, but very thinly populated.
Counties of England.Gwynedd: A Welsh county in the north-west that includes Snowdon, so it counts as Wales, not England.
Counties of England.Antrim: A Northern Irish county, home to the Giant's Causeway, so it is in the UK but not England.
Counties of England.Kerry: An Irish county in the far south-west, famous for its scenic ring road and rugged coast.
Counties of England.Donegal: Part of the Republic of Ireland despite being in the northern province of Ulster, and famed for its tweed.
Counties of England.Perthshire: A traditional Scottish county of lochs and Highland glens, with no connection to English counties.
Counties of England.Pembrokeshire: A Welsh county with a stunning national-park coast, so it fits Wales rather than England.
Counties of England.Aberdeenshire: A Scottish council area full of castles, whose coast is linked to the North Sea oil industry.
Counties of England.Ceredigion: This Welsh county on Cardigan Bay takes its name from the early king Ceredig, and the Welsh form of Cardigan comes from it.
Counties of England.Tipperary: An Irish county made famous by the First World War song "It's a Long Way to Tipperary".

Things the Netherlands is famous for.Windmills: Kinderdijk has 19 windmills, now UNESCO-listed, that once pumped water from low land.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Tulips: Tulip mania of the 1630s saw bulbs sell for the price of a house, though the flowers originally came from Central Asia.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Clogs: Wooden shoes, called klompen, were practical for wet farmland, and still protect workers' feet.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Canals: Amsterdam's 17th-century canal ring is UNESCO-listed, and the city has more bridges than Venice.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Gouda: Named after the town where the cheese was traded, not made, and it is the most widely produced Dutch cheese.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Stroopwafels: Two thin waffles stuck together with caramel syrup, first made in Gouda around 1800.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Bicycles: There are more bicycles than people in the country, and cycling is a way of life.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Van Gogh: The painter sold very few works in his lifetime, and the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam now holds the world's largest collection.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Rembrandt: Painted The Night Watch in 1642, a vast group portrait, and lived and worked in Amsterdam.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Delftware: Blue-and-white pottery from Delft, first made to imitate expensive Chinese porcelain.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Edam: A cheese in red wax rind, which lasts so long it was a staple on ships.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Dykes: About a quarter of the country lies below sea level, protected by dykes and pumps for centuries.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Fondue: The melted-cheese pot is Swiss, a mountain dish for sharing, so it is not Dutch.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Lederhosen: Leather shorts, traditional in Bavaria and Alpine regions, are a Germany and Austria thing, not Dutch.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Paella: This saffron rice dish comes from Valencia in Spain, and was originally cooked over an open fire.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Flamenco: The passionate dance and song of Andalusia in southern Spain, and not part of Dutch tradition.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Kilts: The pleated tartan skirt is Scottish Highland dress, not Dutch, and the Dutch wear clogs instead.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Bagpipes: Scotland's best-known instrument, though pipes exist across Europe, but they are not a Dutch symbol.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Haggis: A Scottish dish of sheep offal with oats and spices, celebrated on Burns Night, not a Dutch one.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Sauna: A Finnish institution, where there are about as many saunas as there are people, so it is not Dutch.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Croissant: A French breakfast icon, though it descends from the Austrian kipferl, so it is not Dutch.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Pretzel: The knotted baked snack is a German and Alpine tradition, and not from the Netherlands.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Yodeling: This singing style flipping between chest and head voice is from the Alps, not the flat Dutch lowlands.
Things the Netherlands is famous for.Matador: A Spanish bullfighter, whose name means killer in Spanish, so this belongs to Spain, not the Netherlands.

Space telescopes (not on the ground).Hubble: Launched in 1990 with a flawed mirror, it was fixed by spacewalking astronauts in 1993 and has since produced some of the most famous images in astronomy.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).James Webb: Launched on Christmas Day 2021, it has a gold-coated, 6.5-meter mirror and a sunshield the size of a tennis court, and it observes in infrared.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Kepler: This planet-hunter stared at one patch of sky from 2009 and found thousands of planets, showing that planets are common around stars.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Spitzer: An infrared observatory that trailed Earth around the Sun from 2003 and helped discover the seven rocky planets of TRAPPIST-1.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Chandra: The NASA X-ray observatory, launched in 1999, sees violent places like black holes and exploding stars, because Earth's air blocks X-rays.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).TESS: It scans nearly the whole sky for transiting planets around bright, nearby stars, so follow-up telescopes can study them in detail.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Gaia: The European mission is mapping about a billion stars in the Milky Way with astonishing precision, and has measured their motion in 3D.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Euclid: The European telescope launched in 2023 to study dark matter and dark energy by imaging billions of galaxies.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Herschel: A European far-infrared observatory of 2009 to 2013, named for the astronomer who found Uranus and infrared light.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Compton: A 1990s gamma-ray observatory named for the Nobel-winning physicist Arthur Compton, which was deliberately brought down in 2000.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Arecibo: This giant dish in Puerto Rico was a radio telescope on the ground until it collapsed in 2020, so it's not in space.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Very Large Array: A radio array of 27 dishes in New Mexico, famous from the film Contact, but it sits on the ground.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Keck: The twin telescopes on Mauna Kea in Hawaii have segmented 10-meter mirrors, but they're ground-based.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Jodrell Bank: A British radio telescope near Manchester, which tracked Sputnik's rocket in 1957, but it stays on the ground.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Palomar: Its 200-inch mirror in California was the world's largest from 1948 for decades, and it's a ground observatory.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).ALMA: A Chilean array of 66 dishes at 5,000 meters, one of the highest observatories on Earth, so it's a ground telescope.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Yerkes: This Wisconsin observatory houses the world's largest refracting telescope, a 40-inch lens, and it is on the ground.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Green Bank: The world's largest fully steerable radio telescope, in West Virginia, sits in a zone where radio signals are restricted.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Lowell: The Arizona observatory where Pluto was discovered in 1930, a ground-based site.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Parkes: An Australian radio dish nicknamed The Dish, which relayed the Apollo 11 moonwalk pictures, though it's on the ground.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Mount Wilson: A California observatory where Hubble found the universe is expanding, a ground site, not an orbiting one.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Hale: The 200-inch telescope at Palomar is named for George Ellery Hale, and it's on a mountain, not in orbit.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Subaru: A Japanese 8.2-meter telescope in Hawaii, ground-based, and known for wide-field images.
Space telescopes (not on the ground).Gemini: Twin 8-meter telescopes in Hawaii and Chile that together cover the whole sky, though both are on the ground.

Real measurement scales in science.Richter: The Richter scale is logarithmic: each whole step is 10 times the shaking and about 32 times the energy. Modern quakes use moment magnitude.
Real measurement scales in science.Beaufort: Admiral Francis Beaufort devised it in 1805 to rate wind by its effect on sails. It now runs from 0 calm to 12 hurricane.
Real measurement scales in science.Mohs: Mohs ranks mineral hardness from talc at 1 to diamond at 10. It is only ordinal: diamond is far more than twice corundum's hardness.
Real measurement scales in science.Fujita: The Fujita scale rates tornadoes from F0 to F5 by the damage they cause, since wind inside a funnel is hard to measure.
Real measurement scales in science.Saffir-Simpson: This scale grades hurricanes from Category 1 to 5 by wind speed, and it is named for an engineer and a hurricane center director.
Real measurement scales in science.Kelvin: Kelvin starts at absolute zero, where molecular motion nearly stops. It has no negative numbers, and no degree sign.
Real measurement scales in science.Celsius: Anders Celsius first set 100 as freezing and 0 as boiling for water; the scale was flipped after his death.
Real measurement scales in science.Fahrenheit: Fahrenheit set 0 at the freezing point of a brine mixture and aimed for about 96 as body temperature. Few countries use it today.
Real measurement scales in science.pH: The pH scale measures acidity from 0 to 14; pure water sits at 7. It is logarithmic, so pH 4 is ten times more acidic than pH 5.
Real measurement scales in science.Scoville: Wilbur Scoville's 1912 test rates chili heat by how much sugar water is needed to dilute it. Pure capsaicin tops 15 million.
Real measurement scales in science.Decibel: The decibel is logarithmic, so 10 dB more is ten times the sound power. It is named for Alexander Graham Bell.
Real measurement scales in science.Freud: Freud was a psychoanalyst, not a scale builder. His ideas are about the mind, and no measurement scale carries his name.
Real measurement scales in science.Einstein: Einstein gave us relativity, and units and constants named after him, but no measurement scale bears his name.
Real measurement scales in science.Galileo: Galileo studied pendulums, falling bodies and the moons of Jupiter, but no scientific scale carries his name.
Real measurement scales in science.Copernicus: Copernicus put the Sun at the center of the universe, but no measurement scale is named after him.
Real measurement scales in science.Edison: Edison invented a lot, yet no scale of his name exists. Even a famous inventor may be absent from the units list.
Real measurement scales in science.Mendel: Mendel's pea experiments founded genetics, and we speak of Mendelian traits, but there is no Mendel scale.
Real measurement scales in science.Pasteur: Pasteur gave us pasteurization and vaccines. His name is on a process, but not on a measurement scale.
Real measurement scales in science.Hawking: Hawking is known for black hole radiation. Hawking radiation is named for him, but no scale is.
Real measurement scales in science.Sagan: Sagan popularized science with Cosmos. Oddly, a 'Sagan unit' exists as a joke for billions, but it is not a real scale.
Real measurement scales in science.Kepler: Kepler's laws describe how planets orbit, and a space telescope carries his name, but no measurement scale does.
Real measurement scales in science.Halley: Halley's name is on a comet, not on a scale. He predicted its 1758 return, years after his own death.
Real measurement scales in science.Fleming: Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 from a mold on a forgotten dish. His name is on no measurement scale.
Real measurement scales in science.Bohr: Bohr gave us the atom model that bears his name, and the unit 'bohr' radius, but no scale of his name.

Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Mercury: Mercury was the Roman messenger god, and the planet, which circles the Sun in about 88 days, got his name for its speed.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Venus: Venus is named for the Roman goddess of love, and it's the only planet named for a female deity among the classical five.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Mars: Mars, the god of war, gave his name to the red planet, whose color resembled blood, and to the month of March.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Jupiter: Jupiter, king of the Roman gods, lends his name to the biggest planet, and it's more massive than all the others combined.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Saturn: Saturn, the Roman god of agriculture, gave us Saturday, and Saturnalia was a festival around December.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Neptune: Neptune is the Roman sea god, and the planet was named after being discovered through mathematics in 1846.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Pluto: Pluto was the Roman god of the underworld, and the name was proposed in 1930 by an 11-year-old girl from Oxford, Venetia Burney.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Uranus: Uranus is the odd one out: it carries the Greek name of the sky god, not the Roman Caelus.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Apollo: Apollo, the Greek god of the sun, music and prophecy, gave his name to NASA's Moon program, which landed 12 people.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Artemis: Artemis was the Greek goddess of the hunt and Apollo's twin sister, and NASA named its Moon return program after her.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Juno: Juno, queen of the Roman gods, lent her name to the NASA probe orbiting Jupiter, matching the myth, in which she looked through clouds to see Jupiter.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Ceres: Ceres is the Roman goddess of grain, and it is also the largest object in the asteroid belt, and a dwarf planet.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Vesta: Vesta, the Roman goddess of the hearth, names the second largest asteroid, and you can see it with the naked eye at times.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Earth: Earth is not named for a god, since its name comes from Old English and Germanic words meaning ground.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Gemini: Gemini is named for the twins Castor and Pollux, and not for a god, so it is a constellation, which also named a NASA program.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Orion: Orion was a mythical hunter, not a god, and the constellation, the spacecraft and the rocket carry his name.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Voyager: Voyager is just an ordinary word for a traveller, with no god behind it, and it names two NASA probes launched in 1977.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Hubble: Hubble is named for astronomer Edwin Hubble, who showed that the universe is expanding.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Kepler: Kepler is named for astronomer Johannes Kepler, whose laws describe the orbits of planets.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Galileo: Galileo is a person, the Italian scientist who spotted Jupiter's four big moons in 1610.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Cassini: Cassini honors the astronomer Giovanni Cassini, who found the gap in Saturn's rings and is named for a man.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Europa: Europa was a Phoenician princess in Greek myth, whom Zeus, in the form of a bull, carried off, so she was mortal, not a god.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Io: Io was a mortal priestess loved by Zeus, who turned her into a cow, so she's not a goddess, and her moon is the most volcanic place known.
Space names taken from Greek or Roman go.Sputnik: Sputnik is Russian for 'satellite' or fellow traveller, and the first one launched in 1957 was not named for a god.

Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Western: Classic American Wild West stories; many were shot in Spain by Italian directors of the 'spaghetti' type.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Horror: Nosferatu in 1922 helped define horror on screen, and the genre has thrived on cheap scares ever since.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Comedy: Slapstick comedy dominated the silent era with Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Musical: The Jazz Singer in 1927 sparked the sound era, and musicals soon followed.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Thriller: Hitchcock said suspense is a bomb under the table the audience knows about.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Documentary: John Grierson coined the term in a 1926 review of Robert Flaherty's Moana.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Film noir: French critics coined 'black film' in 1946 for shadowy postwar crime movies.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Romance: Love stories are one of the oldest genres, from silent days to Titanic.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Science fiction: Georges Melies's 1902 A Trip to the Moon is one of the earliest science fiction films.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Biopic: Short for biographical picture, it dramatizes a real life, like Gandhi or Lincoln.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Mockumentary: A fictional film in documentary style; This Is Spinal Tap in 1984 is the classic.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Rom-com: Its roots lie in 1930s screwball comedy, where couples trade quick insults.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Heist: Rififi in 1955 includes a roughly half-hour silent heist sequence.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Close-up: A close-up is a camera shot, not a genre.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Montage: Montage is an editing technique that Soviet filmmakers like Eisenstein made famous.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Cameo: A cameo is a brief appearance by a famous person, such as Stan Lee in Marvel films.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Sequel: A sequel follows an earlier film; it isn't a genre.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Trailer: Trailers got their name because they originally trailed the main feature.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Blockbuster: The term borrows from WWII bombs able to flatten a city block, and became linked to Jaws in 1975.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Flashback: A flashback is a storytelling device, not a genre.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Voice-over: The theatrical Blade Runner added studio-forced voice-over narration that many fans disliked.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Jump cut: Godard's Breathless in 1960 made the jump cut famous.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Dolly zoom: The dolly zoom was introduced in Hitchcock's Vertigo and appears in Jaws.
Film genres (not filmmaking terms).Storyboard: Storyboards are shot-by-shot drawings, which Disney popularized in the 1930s.

Opera singers.Luciano Pavarotti: His ringing high Cs in La fille du regiment made him famous, and he became the best-known of the Three Tenors.
Opera singers.Plácido Domingo: He has sung over 150 roles, more than any other tenor, and later became a conductor and opera company director.
Opera singers.José Carreras: He fought leukaemia in 1987 and returned to sing, and later joined the Three Tenors at the 1990 World Cup.
Opera singers.Maria Callas: Nicknamed La Divina, she was famed for dramatic intensity and a tempestuous life, and her Medea and Norma are legendary.
Opera singers.Enrico Caruso: An early recording star, his 1902 Vesti la giubba is considered one of the first records to sell a million copies.
Opera singers.Renée Fleming: Nicknamed the people's diva, she sang the US national anthem at the 2014 Super Bowl, a rare moment for opera.
Opera singers.Kiri Te Kanawa: The New Zealand soprano sang at Prince Charles and Lady Diana's wedding in 1981, watched by hundreds of millions.
Opera singers.Montserrat Caballé: The Spanish soprano recorded the duet Barcelona with Freddie Mercury, and it became the anthem of the 1992 Olympics.
Opera singers.Joan Sutherland: Nicknamed La Stupenda, the Australian soprano was famed for dazzling coloratura and her partnership with her husband, conductor Richard Bonynge.
Opera singers.Cecilia Bartoli: The Italian mezzo-soprano is known for reviving Vivaldi and other Baroque music, and for her dazzling speed.
Opera singers.Anna Netrebko: The Russian-born soprano is a major star at La Scala and the Met, and she also holds Austrian citizenship.
Opera singers.Frank Sinatra: The crooner known for My Way and Fly Me to the Moon sang big-band standards, not opera.
Opera singers.Elvis Presley: The King of Rock and Roll loved gospel and sang ballads with an operatic flair, but he was never an opera singer.
Opera singers.Whitney Houston: The singer's I Will Always Love You was a pop and R&B smash, but her training was gospel and pop, not opera.
Opera singers.Celine Dion: A powerhouse pop singer with a massive voice, famed for My Heart Will Go On, but not an opera singer.
Opera singers.Freddie Mercury: A trap. He sang operatic sections in Bohemian Rhapsody and duetted with Caballe, but he was a rock singer with a four-octave range.
Opera singers.Barbra Streisand: A Broadway and pop icon with a huge voice, known for Funny Girl and Evergreen, not an opera singer.
Opera singers.Mariah Carey: A pop star famed for her whistle register and five-octave claims, but her songs are pop, soul and R&B, not opera.
Opera singers.Adele: The British singer won a pile of Grammys with a soulful voice for Rolling in the Deep, but opera was never her style.
Opera singers.Tom Jones: The Welsh star of It's Not Unusual has a booming voice, but built his career on pop and soul, not opera.
Opera singers.Bing Crosby: His White Christmas is the best-selling single of all time, and his smooth baritone is the crooner's, not the opera singer's.
Opera singers.Aretha Franklin: The Queen of Soul came from gospel roots, and her Nessun dorma at the 1998 Grammys was an astonishing last-minute stand-in for Pavarotti.
Opera singers.Julie Andrews: A trap. She trained as a coloratura soprano as a girl and is famed for musicals like Mary Poppins, not for opera.
Opera singers.Michael Bublé: The Canadian crooner is known for swing standards and Christmas albums, with a voice that is jazz-pop, not opera.

Singing voice types.Soprano: Sopranos are the highest standard female voice, and the best-known soprano parts include the Queen of the Night in Mozart's The Magic Flute.
Singing voice types.Alto: Alto comes from the Italian for 'high', since it was once the highest male adult voice, later sung by women.
Singing voice types.Tenor: Tenors are the heroes of opera, and Luciano Pavarotti's high C notes made the voice famous worldwide.
Singing voice types.Bass: The bass is the lowest male voice, and choirs of Russian Orthodox basses are known for notes that seem to rumble the floor.
Singing voice types.Baritone: The baritone sits between tenor and bass and is the most common male voice type.
Singing voice types.Mezzo-soprano: Mezzo means 'half' in Italian, so a mezzo-soprano is a mid-range female voice, between soprano and alto.
Singing voice types.Contralto: The contralto is the lowest and rarest female voice, with a rich, dark tone.
Singing voice types.Countertenor: A countertenor sings in the female alto or soprano range using falsetto, a style that was big in Baroque music.
Singing voice types.Treble: A treble is a boy soprano, the voice heard in many cathedral choirs before it breaks at puberty.
Singing voice types.Allegro: Trap: allegro is a tempo marking meaning fast and lively, not a voice type.
Singing voice types.Forte: Trap: forte is a dynamic marking meaning loud; it does not describe a voice.
Singing voice types.Crescendo: Trap: crescendo means a gradual increase in volume, not a type of singer.
Singing voice types.Cello: Trap: the cello is a bowed string instrument, not a voice, though it is often compared to a baritone.
Singing voice types.Viola: Trap: the viola is a string instrument, slightly bigger than a violin.
Singing voice types.Oboe: Trap: the oboe is a double-reed wind instrument, famous for providing the orchestra's tuning note A.
Singing voice types.Piccolo: Trap: the piccolo is a tiny flute, and its name is Italian for small.
Singing voice types.Timpani: Trap: timpani are tuned orchestral drums, not a voice.
Singing voice types.Staccato: Trap: staccato is a style of playing short, detached notes.
Singing voice types.Andante: Trap: andante is a walking-speed tempo marking, not a voice type.
Singing voice types.Octave: Trap: an octave is an interval of eight notes, but it is not a type of voice.
Singing voice types.Harmony: Trap: harmony is notes sounding together, and can involve all voice types, but it is not itself one.
Singing voice types.Chorus: Trap: a chorus is a group of singers, not a single voice type.
Singing voice types.Duet: Trap: a duet is a piece for two performers, not a voice type.
Singing voice types.Quartet: Trap: a quartet is a group of four, and it can be made of all four voice types.

David Bowie songs.Space Oddity: Released days before the 1969 Apollo 11 launch, it introduced Major Tom, an astronaut who drifts back in later Bowie songs.
David Bowie songs.Heroes: Recorded beside the Berlin Wall in 1977, it was inspired by a couple Bowie saw embracing there. He also cut German and French versions.
David Bowie songs.Starman: Bowie's 1972 Top of the Pops performance, arm draped round guitarist Mick Ronson, is remembered by many British fans as a life-changing moment.
David Bowie songs.Let's Dance: Nile Rodgers produced this 1983 smash, and a then little-known Stevie Ray Vaughan played the bluesy guitar solos.
David Bowie songs.Ashes to Ashes: This 1980 hit revisits Major Tom as a lonely addict, and its costly video, with Bowie in a Pierrot costume, became iconic.
David Bowie songs.Life on Mars?: Bowie began it as a spoof of Frank Sinatra's My Way, whose melody came from the French song Comme d'habitude.
David Bowie songs.Rebel Rebel: A 1974 glam swan song, with Bowie playing the swaggering guitar riff himself rather than leaving it to a session player.
David Bowie songs.Ziggy Stardust: Both a song and the alien rock star of Bowie's 1972 album. He retired the persona on stage in 1973, shocking even his band.
David Bowie songs.Golden Years: Reportedly written with Elvis Presley in mind, though Elvis never recorded it. It opened Bowie's 1976 Station to Station era.
David Bowie songs.The Jean Genie: The riff nods to the Yardbirds, and the title is a pun on writer Jean Genet, though Bowie's character is really a rock-and-roll drifter.
David Bowie songs.Modern Love: A 1983 Let's Dance track with a jaunty Little Richard feel. It found a new audience through the film Frances Ha.
David Bowie songs.Rocket Man: Trap: Elton John's song, with the same space-travel theme as Space Oddity. Taupin's lyrics were inspired by a Ray Bradbury story.
David Bowie songs.Rio: Duran Duran's 1982 hit is named for Rio de Janeiro, and its yacht video was shot in Antigua and Sri Lanka.
David Bowie songs.Tiny Dancer: Elton's 1971 ode to Bernie Taupin's then-girlfriend became a radio staple, and a bus sing-along in Almost Famous revived it.
David Bowie songs.Bohemian Rhapsody: Queen's six-minute epic. Bowie did work with Queen, on Under Pressure, but this one is purely Freddie Mercury's.
David Bowie songs.Purple Rain: Prince's 1984 title track, from a film of the same name. The album spent 24 weeks at number one in the US.
David Bowie songs.Satisfaction: Keith Richards said the riff came to him in his sleep, and he woke to find it half-recorded on a cassette beside his bed.
David Bowie songs.Your Song: Bernie Taupin reportedly wrote the lyrics over breakfast, and Elton set them to music in minutes. It's Elton's, not Bowie's.
David Bowie songs.Blue Monday: New Order's 1983 song became the best-selling 12-inch single ever. Its sleeve was die-cut to look like a floppy disk.
David Bowie songs.Tainted Love: Soft Cell's 1981 synth-pop cover of Gloria Jones's 1964 soul single went to number one across Europe.
David Bowie songs.Don't You Want Me: Human League's 1981 hit was the UK Christmas number one, written after Phil Oakey met a waitress in a cocktail bar.
David Bowie songs.Come On Eileen: Dexys Midnight Runners topped the charts in 1982 on both sides of the Atlantic, famously in dungarees and violin accompaniment.
David Bowie songs.Karma Chameleon: Culture Club's 1983 chart-topper, sung by Boy George, was number one in many countries and a UK million-seller.
David Bowie songs.Perfect Day: Lou Reed's 1972 classic from Transformer, an album Bowie co-produced. That's the trap: Bowie helped make it but didn't write or sing it.

Things that can roar.Tiger: Tigers have a specially structured larynx, and their roar can carry up to about 3 km.
Things that can roar.Jaguar: A jaguar's roar sounds like a series of hoarse coughs, and it's the only roaring big cat in the Americas.
Things that can roar.Leopard: A leopard's call sounds like sawing wood, but leopards do roar as well.
Things that can roar.Jet engine: A jet engine's roar can exceed 140 decibels near the engine, enough to hurt hearing.
Things that can roar.Motorbike: Motorbikes get their roar from short exhaust pipes and big engines.
Things that can roar.Tyrannosaurus: Hunting cheetahs chirp like birds and purr, but they can't roar, and their ears are built to track far prey instead of shouting.
Things that can roar.Stadium crowd: Even among the big-cat group Panthera, the snow leopard can't roar, making soft chuffs, mews and purr-like sounds instead.
Things that can roar.Thunder: Pumas scream, purr and hiss, but they can't roar, even though they're one of the Americas' largest cats.
Things that can roar.Cheetah: A house cat purrs and meows, but its tiny voice box can't produce a roar like its bigger cousins.
Things that can roar.Snow leopard: Lynxes growl, hiss and yowl, but they never roar, and their tufted ears may help them detect faint sounds.
Things that can roar.Puma: An ocelot meows, purrs and growls, but it can't roar, and its spotted coat made it a victim of the fur trade.
Things that can roar.House cat: Mice squeak, and males sing ultrasonic songs to females that humans can't hear.
Things that can roar.Lynx: Giraffes are mostly silent, but they hum at night, at a pitch too low for us to hear easily.
Things that can roar.Ocelot: Butterflies are silent, and taste with their feet, which is why they land on things to test them.
Things that can roar.Mouse: Goldfish don't roar, and their memory lasts months, not the three seconds of the old myth.
Things that can roar.Giraffe: A whisper uses no vocal fold vibration at all, which makes it the opposite of a roar.
Things that can roar.Butterfly: A library is the opposite of a roar, though the first public libraries were often noisy places where readers read aloud.
Things that can roar.Goldfish: A feather is silent, and the fringe on an owl's feather edges lets it fly almost soundlessly.
Things that can roar.Whisper: A snowflake falls without a sound, and a blanket of fresh snow absorbs noise from the whole neighbourhood.
Things that can roar.Library: Rabbits are quiet, but they can scream loudly when terrified, so a roar isn't in their repertoire.
Things that can roar.Feather: A feather is silent, and its design lets owls fly soundlessly.
Things that can roar.Snowflake: A snowflake falls without a sound, and snow absorbs noise.
Things that can roar.Rabbit: Rabbits are quiet, though they can scream when terrified.

Roman gods.Jupiter: King of the Roman gods, ruler of sky and thunder. The biggest planet carries his name, and his temple stood on the Capitoline Hill.
Roman gods.Juno: Queen of the gods and guardian of marriage. The month of June is named for her, and June is still a favored time to wed.
Roman gods.Mars: God of war, and father of Romulus and Remus in legend. March is named for him, as was the Roman campaign season.
Roman gods.Venus: Goddess of love and beauty. Romans believed she was ancestor of Julius Caesar's family, so she mattered politically.
Roman gods.Mercury: Messenger of the gods, with winged sandals. The fast planet and the quicksilver element both bear his name.
Roman gods.Neptune: God of the sea, and brother of Jupiter. The farthest planet is named for him, which was discovered in 1846.
Roman gods.Minerva: Goddess of wisdom, crafts and strategy. She is often shown with an owl, which became a symbol of learning.
Roman gods.Vulcan: God of fire and metalworking. Volcanoes take their name from him, and Romans believed his forge sat beneath Mount Etna.
Roman gods.Diana: Goddess of the hunt, the moon and forests. She guarded women and wild animals, and the Greek twin is Artemis.
Roman gods.Ceres: Goddess of grain and harvest. The word cereal comes from her name, and a dwarf planet is named for her too.
Roman gods.Janus: A two-faced god of doorways, beginnings and endings. January is named for him because it opens the year.
Roman gods.Saturn: God of agriculture, honored in the festival of Saturnalia in December. That party of gift-giving and role reversal helped shape later midwinter traditions.
Roman gods.Bacchus: God of wine and revelry. His Greek form is Dionysus, and the Bacchanalia festivals alarmed the Roman Senate in 186 BC.
Roman gods.Zeus: The Greek king of gods and the Greek match for Jupiter. He is a trap here, since the Roman list uses Latin names.
Roman gods.Hera: The Greek queen of the gods, matching Juno. Her Greek name makes her a miss on a Roman list.
Roman gods.Ares: The Greek war god, matching Mars. Romans saw Mars as more dignified, a founder's father, than Ares was to the Greeks.
Roman gods.Athena: The Greek goddess of wisdom, whom Romans called Minerva. So the Greek name is the wrong match.
Roman gods.Hermes: The Greek messenger god, known to the Romans as Mercury. The Greek name is the trap, since this list uses Latin names.
Roman gods.Odin: The Norse all-father, who gave an eye for wisdom. He belongs to Scandinavian mythology and not Rome.
Roman gods.Isis: An Egyptian goddess of magic and motherhood. Her cult spread across the Roman Empire, though she wasn't one of its native gods.
Roman gods.Thor: The Norse god of thunder with a hammer. Thursday is named after him, and he is a Scandinavian figure and not a Roman god.
Roman gods.Poseidon: The Greek sea god, who matches the Roman Neptune. His Greek name makes him a miss on a list of Roman gods.
Roman gods.Horus: The Egyptian falcon-headed sky god, son of Isis and Osiris. The Eye of Horus is a famous symbol of protection.
Roman gods.Artemis: The Greek goddess of the hunt, matching the Roman Diana. Her Greek name means she does not belong on this Roman list.

On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Hector: Troy's best fighter and Priam's eldest son. His death at Achilles' hands, and the dragging of his body, ends the Iliad's story.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Paris: The Trojan prince who took Helen from Sparta, starting the war. He was reportedly given the choice of the fairest goddess.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Priam: The aging king of Troy, who braved the Greek camp to beg Achilles for his son Hector's body.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Aeneas: A Trojan hero who escaped with his father on his back, and by Virgil's tale founded the line that led to Rome.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Sarpedon: A Lycian prince fighting for Troy and a son of Zeus, who was killed by Patroclus. Zeus wept bloody rain.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Memnon: King of Ethiopia and son of the dawn goddess Eos, he came to aid Troy and was killed by Achilles.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Penthesilea: An Amazon queen who came to help Troy after Hector's death. Achilles killed her, and reportedly fell for her as she died.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Troilus: A young Trojan prince killed by Achilles. Chaucer and Shakespeare later made him a lover of Cressida.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Deiphobus: A Trojan prince who married Helen after Paris died. In the Odyssey, Menelaus kills him in the sack of Troy.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Hecuba: Priam's queen who saw many of her children die. In some stories she was turned into a dog after the fall of Troy.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Cassandra: Priam's daughter, cursed by Apollo to speak true prophecy that nobody believed. She warned of the Horse in vain.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Andromache: Hector's wife, who saw him killed. After Troy's fall she was taken as a captive by Achilles' son.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Achilles: A trap: he is the greatest Greek warrior, who came with the Greek army and killed Hector.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Agamemnon: King of Mycenae and leader of the whole Greek expedition. His quarrel with Achilles opens the Iliad.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Menelaus: King of Sparta and Helen's husband, so the Greek side. He wanted his wife back.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Odysseus: The cunning Greek who devised the wooden horse to finally take Troy.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Ajax: A towering Greek hero and the best fighter after Achilles. He took his own life after losing a contest for Achilles' armor.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Diomedes: A Greek king who, helped by Athena, wounded Aphrodite and Ares in battle.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Patroclus: Achilles' dearest companion. He was killed by Hector wearing Achilles' armor, bringing Achilles back into the fight.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Nestor: The oldest Greek commander, famed for wise advice and long-winded stories. His wisdom made his name a byword for sage counsel.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Philoctetes: A Greek archer who owned Heracles' bow, and was abandoned on an island with a snake wound. The Greeks needed his bow to win.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Neoptolemus: Achilles' young son, brought into the war late. He killed King Priam during the sack of Troy.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Calchas: The Greeks' seer, who advised the sacrifice of Iphigenia. Greek, not Trojan.
On Troy's side in the Trojan War.Idomeneus: King of Crete and a leader of the Greek forces, said to have sent eighty ships to the war.

Creatures of Japanese folklore.Kitsune: Fox spirits who grow extra tails with age, up to nine, and can shapeshift; they're also messengers of the rice god Inari.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Tengu: Long-nosed or beaked mountain goblins, who were once seen as omens of war, later guardians of mountains and teachers of swordsmen.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Kappa: A river imp with a water-filled dish on its head; if you bow, it bows back and the water spills, weakening it.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Oni: Horned ogres in tiger-skin loincloths; at Setsubun, people throw soybeans to drive them out of the home.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Tanuki: Real raccoon dogs are also shapeshifters in lore, with leaves on their head and big bellies, shown outside restaurants.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Yuki-onna: The Snow Woman, a pale ghost in white who appears in blizzards; Lafcadio Hearn made the tale well known to the West.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Baku: A tapir-like dream eater, which can be called on to swallow nightmares.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Rokurokubi: A woman by day whose neck stretches long at night, often seen peering over rooms.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Bakeneko: A cat that grows old and gains powers, standing on its hind legs and shapeshifting; its tail may split in two, becoming a nekomata.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Kodama: Tree spirits, whose echoes in the woods are believed to be their voices; Princess Mononoke features them as white forest sprites.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Banshee: A trap: this wailing death-omen is Irish, and Irish folklore doesn't mix with Japanese yokai.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Leprechaun: A trap: the gold-guarding shoemaker fairy belongs to Irish folklore, not Japan.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Djinn: A trap: these Arabian spirits are made of smokeless fire, and come from Islamic-era lore, not Japan.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Golem: A trap: the clay figure brought to life is from Jewish folklore, with the famous tale set in Prague.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Baba Yaga: A trap: the witch with a hut on chicken legs is Slavic, not Japanese.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Wendigo: A trap: a cannibal spirit from Algonquian tales in North America, not Japan.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Chupacabra: A trap: this modern cryptid was first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995, long after Japanese yokai tales.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Kelpie: A trap: the shape-shifting water horse is Scottish, unlike Japan's river kappa.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Troll: A trap: Scandinavian trolls turn to stone in sunlight, and aren't Japanese yokai.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Yeti: A trap: the Himalayan snowman is from Tibetan and Nepali lore, not Japanese folklore.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Bunyip: A trap: this swamp creature belongs to Aboriginal Australian tradition, not to Japan.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Krampus: A trap: the horned beast from Alpine Christmas folklore punishes naughty children in Austria, not Japan.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Gremlin: A trap: this mischief-maker was invented by British RAF pilots around the 1920s to blame machine faults.
Creatures of Japanese folklore.Bigfoot: A trap: the Sasquatch of North American forests is cryptid lore from the Pacific Northwest, not Japan.

Ancient sites in Egypt.Giza: The Great Pyramid's plateau near Cairo, with three main pyramids. Khufu's, about 4,500 years old, was the tallest human-made structure for nearly four millennia.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Abu Simbel: Ramesses II carved two colossal temples into a cliff here. In the 1960s, they were moved piece by piece to save them from Lake Nasser.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Karnak: A huge temple complex at Luxor, built across about 2,000 years. Its Hypostyle Hall has 134 giant columns.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Luxor Temple: A temple on the Nile in the middle of modern Luxor, linked to Karnak by a road lined with sphinxes.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Valley of the Kings: A hidden royal burial ground near Luxor, holding Tutankhamun's tomb found in 1922, along with about sixty others.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Saqqara: A necropolis near Cairo, home to the Step Pyramid, the oldest large stone building, designed by Imhotep.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Philae: A temple island on the Nile dedicated to Isis. It was moved to a nearby island in the 1970s to avoid flooding.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Edfu: One of the best-preserved temples in Egypt, dedicated to Horus. Its walls are covered in inscriptions.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Dendera: A temple to Hathor, whose ceiling shows a famous zodiac. The temple is remarkably complete.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Memphis: The first capital of unified Egypt, founded about 3100 BC. Little remains of it today beyond a colossal statue.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Amarna: Akhenaten's short-lived capital, built to honour the sun-disc Aten. It was abandoned after his death.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Abydos: A sacred site where Osiris was said to be buried, with the Temple of Seti I. It contains a famous king list.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Petra: Trap: a Jordanian city carved into rose-red cliffs by the Nabataeans. Beautiful, but not Egyptian.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Persepolis: Trap: a ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire in modern Iran. Persia conquered Egypt, but the city is in Iran.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Babylon: Trap: the Mesopotamian city in modern Iraq, famous for its legendary gardens. Not in Egypt.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Ur: Trap: a Sumerian city in Iraq with a surviving ziggurat. It is thought to be Abraham's birthplace in tradition.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Leptis Magna: Trap: a Roman city on the Libyan coast with some of the best-preserved ruins. Birthplace of Emperor Septimius Severus.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Meroe: Trap: a Kushite city in Sudan with more pyramids than Egypt. Close to Egypt, but in Sudan.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Timbuktu: Trap: a Malian city once famed as a centre for trade and Islamic learning, far from Egypt in West Africa.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Baalbek: Trap: a site in Lebanon with some of the largest Roman temple stones ever cut. Not in Egypt.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Ephesus: Trap: a Greek and Roman city in Turkey, once home to the Temple of Artemis, a wonder of the ancient world.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Jerash: Trap: a Jordanian city with remarkably well-preserved Roman ruins, but it's not in Egypt.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Palmyra: Trap: a Syrian oasis city whose Queen Zenobia challenged Rome in the 270s. Not an Egyptian site.
Ancient sites in Egypt.Carthage: Trap: a Phoenician city in Tunisia, famed for Hannibal. It is in North Africa, but not in Egypt.

Things you keep in a wallet.Credit card: The first universal charge card, Diners Club, appeared in 1950 after founder Frank McNamara reportedly forgot his wallet at dinner.
Things you keep in a wallet.Cash: The US dollar bill is a cotton-and-linen blend rather than wood-pulp paper, and lasts only about six or seven years.
Things you keep in a wallet.Driver's license: Britain made licenses mandatory in 1903, with no driving test at all; the test only arrived in 1934.
Things you keep in a wallet.Receipt: Stashed receipts often fade because heat-sensitive thermal paper darkens only where it was printed.
Things you keep in a wallet.Gift card: Surveys regularly find large balances left unspent on gift cards, a windfall for retailers.
Things you keep in a wallet.ID card: Estonia's ID cards let citizens sign documents and vote online, a pioneering digital system.
Things you keep in a wallet.Library card: Andrew Carnegie funded over 2,500 libraries, many of which issued cards just like it.
Things you keep in a wallet.Business card: Its ancestor was the 17th-century 'visiting card' that European aristocrats left at one another's homes.
Things you keep in a wallet.Debit card: Most debit and credit cards use an embedded chip that creates a unique code for each transaction.
Things you keep in a wallet.Passport photo: Many countries ban smiling in photos because facial-recognition systems work best with a neutral expression.
Things you keep in a wallet.Stapler: Too chunky for a billfold; its spring-loaded driver pushes the staple through paper and bends the legs closed.
Things you keep in a wallet.Toothbrush: The first mass-produced nylon-bristled toothbrush appeared in 1938; earlier ones used boar hair.
Things you keep in a wallet.Umbrella: Too long; 'umbrella' comes from Latin umbra, meaning shade.
Things you keep in a wallet.Laptop: The 1981 Osborne 1, a 'portable' computer, weighed about 11 kilograms; no wallet for that.
Things you keep in a wallet.Hairbrush: The old advice to brush 100 strokes nightly is a myth, and may actually damage hair.
Things you keep in a wallet.Banana: Bananas are slightly radioactive thanks to potassium-40, a favorite physics joke, but they don't fit in a wallet.
Things you keep in a wallet.Spoon: 'Born with a silver spoon' goes back to the custom of giving silver spoons as christening gifts.
Things you keep in a wallet.Shoe: The oldest known leather shoe, found in an Armenian cave, is about 5,500 years old.
Things you keep in a wallet.Mug: Slang 'mug' for a face probably comes from 1700s drinking mugs shaped like grotesque faces.
Things you keep in a wallet.Pillow: The oldest pillows, from ancient Mesopotamia, were made of stone.
Things you keep in a wallet.Candle: Candles marked with rings once served as simple clocks, burning down at a roughly steady pace.
Things you keep in a wallet.Remote control: The first universal remote, Steve Wozniak's CL 9 Core of 1987, was still far bigger than a wallet.
Things you keep in a wallet.Scarf: Roman cloth worn at the neck, the focale, is an early ancestor of the scarf.
Things you keep in a wallet.Kettle: Early electric kettles in the 1890s were slow because the heating element sat in a separate chamber.

Things that still work in a power cut.Flashlight: Battery flashlights date to 1899, and the early ones gave only short flashes, hence the British term 'torch'.
Things that still work in a power cut.Candles: A candle's wick draws melted wax upward by capillary action, which is why the flame keeps burning steadily.
Things that still work in a power cut.Matches: Strike-anywhere matches arrived in the 1820s, and the 'safety match' later kept the chemicals on the box instead.
Things that still work in a power cut.Power bank: A power bank stores charge in lithium-ion cells, and can usually top up a phone one to three times.
Things that still work in a power cut.Battery radio: Battery radios are valuable in emergencies since AM and FM broadcasts keep running when other systems fail.
Things that still work in a power cut.Headlamp: A headlamp leaves both hands free, which is why climbers, cavers, and runners rely on them.
Things that still work in a power cut.Camping lantern: Modern LED lanterns can run for dozens of hours on a set of batteries.
Things that still work in a power cut.Glow sticks: A glow stick shines when two chemicals mix after you snap the inner vial, no battery needed, and the light doesn't generate heat.
Things that still work in a power cut.Wind-up radio: Trevor Baylis invented the clockwork radio in the 1990s to spread health news in Africa, no batteries needed.
Things that still work in a power cut.Gas camping stove: Canister stoves burn pressurized butane or propane, and they can heat water for hot drinks anywhere.
Things that still work in a power cut.Hand-crank torch: Cranking spins a small generator, or charges a capacitor, and gives a minute of light for a minute of cranking.
Things that still work in a power cut.Board games: Board games are the original no-electricity entertainment, and Senet from ancient Egypt is among the oldest known.
Things that still work in a power cut.Microwave: It needs mains power to run its magnetron, which is the part that makes the microwaves, so it stops at once.
Things that still work in a power cut.Electric kettle: Without mains power, an electric kettle's element is useless, so you'd need a stovetop kettle on a gas flame.
Things that still work in a power cut.Television: A TV can't run without mains power, but a battery-powered portable one used to be a camping gadget.
Things that still work in a power cut.Desk lamp: A trap: a plugged-in desk lamp goes dark in a power cut, while a battery or rechargeable lamp would carry on.
Things that still work in a power cut.Hair dryer: A hair dryer draws a lot of power, often over 1,000 watts, which is why it goes dead during an outage.
Things that still work in a power cut.Toaster: Toasters rely on a heating element drawing mains power, and the pop-up spring is the only thing that keeps working.
Things that still work in a power cut.Electric heater: A heater needs lots of electricity, so in a blackout, it's useless just when the room gets cold.
Things that still work in a power cut.Wi-Fi router: A router needs power to send a signal, so even if your phone works, the home Wi-Fi goes down.
Things that still work in a power cut.Blender: A blender's motor needs mains electricity, so a hand whisk is the old-fashioned alternative.
Things that still work in a power cut.Dishwasher: A dishwasher needs electricity for its pump and heater, so a power cut leaves the dishes dirty.
Things that still work in a power cut.Air fryer: An air fryer is a small convection oven, with a heating element and fan that both need mains power.
Things that still work in a power cut.Electric stove: An electric stove goes cold in an outage, unlike gas hobs that can often be lit with a match.

Things you'd use to hang a picture.Nail: A small nail at a slight upward angle can bear surprising weight, and it holds in the wall better than straight.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Hammer: A small hammer helps drive picture nails in, and tapping gently avoids cracking plaster.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Picture hook: Picture hooks often hold a nail at an angle, and a hook rated for a weight may carry far more than a bare nail.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Spirit level: A bubble in the vial sits between two lines when the level is flat, and it works in any orientation.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Screw: Screws grip the wall by their threads, and they hold far better than nails in heavy frames.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Wall plug: The plug expands as the screw enters, gripping the inside of a hole in masonry or plasterboard.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Drill: A drill makes a pilot hole, and a masonry bit has a hardened tip that crushes brick or concrete.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Picture wire: Picture wire is twisted steel strands, and it spreads a frame's weight across two points on its back.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Pencil: Pencil marks show the hook position, and they're easily rubbed off the wall.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Tape measure: Measuring the center helps hang pictures at eye level, usually about 145 centimeters from the floor to the middle.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Stud finder: A stud finder senses changes in density or magnetism, letting you anchor heavy frames in a wooden beam.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Screwdriver: A screwdriver turns screws into the wall, and the right tip size prevents stripped heads.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Adhesive strips: Adhesive strips peel off cleanly when you stretch them straight down, which leaves the wall unharmed.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Whisk: Whisks are for beating air into eggs and cream; on a wall, its only talent would be as a quirky kitchen-themed hook.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Ladle: A ladle is built to scoop soup, and a hook-shaped handle would at best hold a hat, not a framed picture.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Plunger: Suction would hold a feather-light card, but a plunger's rubber cup can't carry a framed picture's weight for long.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Spatula: Spatulas flip and scrape; their flat blades can't bear a frame's weight or drive in a nail.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Toaster: A toaster does one job, heating bread, and no picture-hanging step needs it.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Mop: A mop is for floors, and the wall around a hung picture is the last place you'd want to drag a wet one.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Colander: A colander is full of holes by design, which is great for draining pasta and no help in holding up a frame.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Tongs: Tongs grip food from a distance, and they can't drive a nail or support a frame.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Rolling pin: A rolling pin flattens dough, and using it to tap a nail in risks bent nails and a dented wall.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Sponge: A sponge is for wiping, and the only link to hanging a picture is cleaning smudges off the wall afterward.
Things you'd use to hang a picture.Kettle: A kettle boils water, and steam near a hung picture can curl the paper, so keep them apart.

Things that can run on gasoline.Lawnmower: Small gasoline mower engines are famously dirty: an hour of mowing can pollute about as much as driving a modern car for a long trip.
Things that can run on gasoline.Car: Gasoline was once a waste byproduct of refining kerosene for lamps; the car boom turned it into the main product of oil refineries.
Things that can run on gasoline.Motorcycle: Gottlieb Daimler's 1885 wooden 'Reitwagen' was the first gasoline-powered motorcycle, with a single cylinder and wooden wheels.
Things that can run on gasoline.Chainsaw: Early chainsaws were not for trees at all: doctors used a similar chain device in the 1780s to cut bone during childbirth.
Things that can run on gasoline.Leaf blower: Leaf blowers began in 1970s Japan, and some cities now ban gasoline ones because the two-stroke engines are so loud and polluting.
Things that can run on gasoline.Generator: Many portable generators burn gasoline, but it spoils in a few months, so stored fuel often needs a stabilizer to start reliably.
Things that can run on gasoline.Moped: The name blends 'motor' and 'pedal': early mopeds had bicycle pedals to help start the small engine or climb hills.
Things that can run on gasoline.Jet ski: Jet ski is a brand name from Kawasaki; the craft has no propeller and is pushed by a water jet pumped out the back.
Things that can run on gasoline.Snowmobile: Canadian Joseph-Armand Bombardier developed the snowmobile in the 1930s and 1950s to carry rural patients through deep winter snow.
Things that can run on gasoline.Outboard motor: Ole Evinrude invented the outboard in 1909 after his ice cream melted while rowing to fetch it for his sweetheart.
Things that can run on gasoline.Go-kart: The first go-kart was built in 1956 in California by Art Ingels, an aircraft racer who used a lawnmower engine and scrap tubing.
Things that can run on gasoline.Bicycle: A bicycle runs on food, and it is the most energy-efficient way for a person to travel, far better per mile than walking.
Things that can run on gasoline.Toaster: Toasters run on electricity, and the first widely sold pop-up model of 1926 used a timer to stop the bread from burning.
Things that can run on gasoline.Hair dryer: Hair dryers run on electricity; the first ones, from the 1890s, were French salon gadgets that blew heated air from a gas stove.
Things that can run on gasoline.Skateboard: Skateboards began in 1950s California when surfers added roller-skate wheels to planks for 'sidewalk surfing' on flat-water days.
Things that can run on gasoline.Kick scooter: Kick scooters are muscle-powered, but their electric cousins are now so common that many cities have set speed limits for them.
Things that can run on gasoline.Rowboat: Rowboats are the textbook example of human power; rowers face backward, which is why they steer by glancing over a shoulder.
Things that can run on gasoline.Sailboat: Sailboats can't sail straight into the wind, but by zigzagging they can make progress upwind, a trick called tacking.
Things that can run on gasoline.Microwave: The microwave oven came from a radar engineer, Percy Spencer, who noticed in 1945 that a candy bar had melted in his pocket.
Things that can run on gasoline.Television: Televisions run on electricity; the old cathode-ray tube sets fired a beam of electrons that painted the picture line by line.
Things that can run on gasoline.Kettle: Electric kettles boil water faster than a stovetop kettle because the heating element sits directly in the water.
Things that can run on gasoline.Treadmill: Treadmills began in 1818 as a Victorian prison punishment, with convicts walking a giant wheel to grind grain or pump water.
Things that can run on gasoline.Roller skates: Roller skates were reportedly first shown in 1760 by a Belgian inventor who crashed into a mirror while playing violin on them.
Things that can run on gasoline.Tricycle: A tricycle needs no fuel, but the word does mean 'three wheels': the same Greek roots as in 'tripod' and 'trio'.

Things you'd find in a briefcase.Laptop: The first portable laptops of the 1980s weighed more than 10 pounds, and today they fit comfortably in a slim case.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Documents: Briefcases were first designed to carry papers, and the word 'brief' meant a legal document in the 1800s.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Pens: Ballpoint pens were popularized in the 1940s and the Biro, named for its inventor, gave us the British word for them.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Calculator: The slim solar-powered models of the 1980s suited a briefcase, and the sliding slide rule came before it.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Business cards: Business cards began as 17th century French visiting cards, and the Japanese exchange them with a bow and two hands.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Planner: Paper planners stay popular despite phones, and many people find writing a task makes them more likely to do it.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.File folder: The manila folder is named after hemp fiber from Manila, and the vertical filing cabinet came in the 1890s.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Reading glasses: Eyeglasses appeared in Italy in the late 1200s, and almost everyone needs reading glasses after about age 45.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Phone charger: A charger is a modern briefcase essential, and many people keep a spare cable in the bag.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Notepad: The yellow legal pad was invented in 1888 by a Massachusetts papermaker, Thomas Holley, using paper scraps.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Sticky notes: Post-its came from a failed glue made by Spencer Silver at 3M in 1968, until Art Fry used it for hymnal bookmarks.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Contract: Contracts are among the oldest written records, and Sumerian clay tablets recorded trades about 5,000 years ago.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Bowling ball: A bowling ball weighs up to 16 pounds, which would break most briefcase clasps.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Toaster: A toaster is big and awkward, and the first electric one went on sale in 1909.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Watermelon: Watermelon is about 92 percent water, and it makes a very messy briefcase.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Frying pan: A frying pan is a kitchen item, and there is no way you could slide it into a slim case.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Goldfish: Goldfish need water, so you would find one in a tank and not a briefcase.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Garden hose: A garden hose coiled up might physically fit, but it belongs in the shed.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Basketball: A basketball is too round and big to fit in a briefcase, at about 24 centimeters across.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Kettle: A kettle is a kitchen tool, and a briefcase that held one would be very heavy and spill.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Car tire: A car tire weighs about 10 kilograms and is far wider than any briefcase.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Potted cactus: A potted cactus is prickly, and one in a briefcase would pierce the papers.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Garden gnome: Garden gnomes first appeared in Germany in the 1800s, and they live in gardens, not in a briefcase.
Things you'd find in a briefcase.Bag of cement: A cement bag weighs 25 to 50 kilograms, which would tear the handle off any briefcase.

Jobs on a film set.Director: The director guides the whole creative vision, yet in early cinema many also operated the camera themselves.
Jobs on a film set.Gaffer: The gaffer is the chief electrician who runs the lighting crew; the term may come from the gaff pole once used to adjust lamps.
Jobs on a film set.Best boy: The best boy is the assistant to the gaffer or key grip, and the title has nothing to do with gender: best girls exist on sets too.
Jobs on a film set.Grip: A grip builds and moves the camera supports, rigs and dollies, and the key grip often invents clever rigs on the spot.
Jobs on a film set.Boom operator: The boom operator holds a microphone on a long pole just outside the frame, and is often the person on the crew with the strongest arms.
Jobs on a film set.Script supervisor: The script supervisor tracks continuity, making sure a coffee cup or an actor's hair matches from shot to shot across days of filming.
Jobs on a film set.Cinematographer: The cinematographer, or director of photography, designs the look of the film's light and framing, with real power over its mood.
Jobs on a film set.Stunt double: Stunt doubles take falls, fights and crashes in place of actors, and the work is carefully choreographed and rehearsed.
Jobs on a film set.Makeup artist: Makeup artists can transform actors with prosthetics, and on some films the application takes hours before shooting begins.
Jobs on a film set.Clapper loader: The clapper loader loads film magazines and operates the clapperboard that syncs picture and sound, and the snap is its signature.
Jobs on a film set.Producer: Producers raise money and manage the project from the first idea to release, and their name is on the Best Picture Oscar.
Jobs on a film set.Usher: Projectionists show films in a cinema, so they work at the end of the chain, not on the set.
Jobs on a film set.Projectionist: Ushers guide audiences in theatres and cinemas, and they work out front, never on the film set itself.
Jobs on a film set.Ticket taker: Ticket takers check admissions at the cinema door, again an audience-side job, not part of making the film.
Jobs on a film set.Film critic: Film critics review finished movies. They work after the shoot, and some sets even ban them from visiting.
Jobs on a film set.Prompter: A prompter feeds forgotten lines to stage actors, so it's a theatre job; film uses cue cards and retakes instead.
Jobs on a film set.Librarian: Librarians look after books and archives, which is a quiet world away from a noisy set.
Jobs on a film set.Croupier: Croupiers deal casino games. A film about gambling may hire one as an adviser, but they aren't normal crew.
Jobs on a film set.Jockey: Jockeys ride racehorses. A film about racing may hire real ones, but they're not a standard set job.
Jobs on a film set.Auctioneer: Auctioneers sell items at a fast chant, so they're part of a sale room, not a film crew.
Jobs on a film set.Popcorn seller: Popcorn sellers work at cinemas to serve audiences, and the snack became a movie staple during the Great Depression.
Jobs on a film set.Organist: Organists once played live accompaniment to silent films in cinemas, so they were audience-side, not on set.
Jobs on a film set.Lifeguard: Lifeguards watch over swimmers, though a film shooting a water scene may hire a safety diver or two for the crew.
Jobs on a film set.Sommelier: Sommeliers advise on wine at restaurants, so they'd only turn up on a film set as an actor playing one.

Jobs driving road vehicles.Taxi driver: London black cab drivers memorise some 25,000 streets for 'The Knowledge', a test that can take years.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Truck driver: Tachographs record driving time in many countries, so rest breaks are enforced and not just suggested.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Bus driver: Rosa Parks's 1955 protest began on a Montgomery bus when its driver ordered her to give up her seat.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Chauffeur: The word is French for stoker, from days when steam cars needed someone to tend the fire.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Racing driver: A Formula 1 driver can sweat off several kilograms in a hot race while enduring heavy cornering forces.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Delivery driver: UPS famously planned routes to avoid left turns, cutting idling time and saving fuel.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Tow truck driver: The first tow truck was built in 1916 in Chattanooga by Ernest Holmes, after he hauled a car out of a creek.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Ambulance driver: Ernest Hemingway served as a Red Cross ambulance driver in Italy in 1918, which inspired A Farewell to Arms.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Valet: From French for a gentleman's manservant, the word now also means someone who parks your car, so it fits.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Pilot: Pilots fly aircraft, so no road is involved; the word was first used for ship steersmen, long before airplanes.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Sailor: Crews a boat on water; sailors steer ships but aren't said to drive them.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Jockey: Rides a horse, which isn't a vehicle; the word derives from Jock, the Scottish form of Jack.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Astronaut: Apollo 15's crew drove a lunar rover in 1971, but the job is spaceflight, and the moon has no roads.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Train conductor: Checks tickets and oversees the train; the engineer, called a driver in the UK, does the driving, but on rails.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Gondolier: Poles a Venetian boat, not a road vehicle; Venice licenses only a few hundred gondoliers.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Coxswain: Steers a rowing boat and calls the stroke, so it's a water role; the cox is usually the smallest on board.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Ferryman: In Greek myth, Charon ferried the dead over the river Styx for a coin, but a ferryman handles boats, not roads.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Flight attendant: Serves and protects passengers in the air; the first ones, in 1930, were nurses hired by Boeing Air Transport.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Helmsman: Steers a ship by the helm; the word traces to the Old English for rudder handle, nothing road-bound.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Signalman: Operates railway signals and points to keep trains apart; it's a rail job, not driving.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Lifeguard: Watches swimmers rather than driving; the world's first surf lifesaving club formed at Bondi in 1907.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Canoeist: Paddles a human-powered boat; canoe sprint has been an Olympic sport since 1936.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Stationmaster: Runs a railway station, an administrative rail job that involves no driving at all.
Jobs driving road vehicles.Harbour pilot: Guides big ships into port using local knowledge, and boards from a pilot boat by rope ladder.
