Owned by Amazon.Audible: Amazon acquired the audiobook giant in 2008 for roughly $300 million.
Owned by Amazon.Ring: Started as Doorbot; Amazon bought it in 2018 for a reported $1 billion or more.
Owned by Amazon.Whole Foods: Amazon bought the grocer in 2017 for $13.7 billion, its largest deal ever.
Owned by Amazon.Zappos: Amazon bought it in 2009 for over $1 billion; it's known for free returns and quirky service.
Owned by Amazon.IMDb: Started in 1990 as a fan-run list on Usenet; Amazon bought it in 1998.
Owned by Amazon.Kindle: The first Kindle launched in 2007 and sold out in about five hours.
Owned by Amazon.Alexa: Reportedly named partly for its hard consonant and partly as a nod to the Library of Alexandria.
Owned by Amazon.AWS: Amazon's cloud arm, launched in 2006, is its biggest profit engine.
Owned by Amazon.Goodreads: A reader social site that Amazon bought in 2013, with millions of members sharing reviews and reading lists.
Owned by Amazon.Fire TV: Amazon's streaming stick and smart TV line since 2014, which put Alexa on the living room screen.
Owned by Amazon.Eero: A mesh Wi-Fi maker that Amazon bought in 2019 to bolster its smart-home lineup around Alexa.
Owned by Amazon.Netflix: Founded in 1997 as a DVD-by-mail service, it's still independent of Amazon, whose rival is Prime Video.
Owned by Amazon.Hulu: Disney holds the majority of this streaming service, not Amazon.
Owned by Amazon.Spotify: A Swedish company, independent of Amazon, whose main rival is Apple Music; Amazon runs its own Music service.
Owned by Amazon.YouTube: Google owns it, purchased in 2006 for $1.65 billion; Amazon's video rival Prime Video came later.
Owned by Amazon.eBay: Founded in 1995 as a hobbyist auction site, it is independent of Amazon and still a rival.
Owned by Amazon.Etsy: An independent marketplace for handmade goods, founded in 2005, and a smaller competitor to Amazon Handmade.
Owned by Amazon.Walmart: The world's largest retailer by revenue, and a big rival to Amazon in groceries and online shopping.
Owned by Amazon.Instagram: Meta owns Instagram, which it bought in 2012 for $1 billion; Amazon has no stake.
Owned by Amazon.Roomba: Amazon tried to buy maker iRobot for $1.7 billion, but the deal collapsed in early 2024 over EU concerns.
Owned by Amazon.Shazam: Apple bought it in 2018; in the UK it began as a service where you dialed 2580 to identify songs.
Owned by Amazon.Fitbit: Google bought the fitness tracker maker in 2021 for about $2 billion, so it isn't Amazon's.
Owned by Amazon.Waze: Google bought the navigation app in 2013 for about $1.1 billion, so it isn't Amazon's.

Invented before the World Wide Web.Fax machine: Scottish inventor Alexander Bain patented a fax-like device in 1843, decades before the telephone.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Telephone: Alexander Graham Bell patented it in 1876, over a century before the Web.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Television: Scottish engineer John Logie Baird first demonstrated television in the 1920s.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Walkman: Sony's 1979 portable cassette player; Sony's chairman Akio Morita pushed for the personal stereo concept.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Microwave oven: Percy Spencer noticed a chocolate bar melting near a radar magnetron in 1945, which led to the oven.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Pager: Doctors used these beepers from the 1950s, long before smartphones existed.
Invented before the World Wide Web.VCR: The Betamax versus VHS format war of the 1980s was won by VHS, mostly thanks to longer recording times.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Floppy disk: IBM introduced it in 1971 as an 8-inch disk, and its image is still the save icon today.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Email: Predates the Web by two decades; Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked message in 1971.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Mobile phone: Martin Cooper made the first handheld mobile call in 1973 on a Motorola prototype.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Compact disc: Launched in 1982 by Sony and Philips; Billy Joel's 52nd Street was among the first released.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Barcode: The first scanned item was a pack of Wrigley's gum in 1974 at an Ohio supermarket.
Invented before the World Wide Web.iPod: Launched in 2001, long after the Web was public, and it killed off the clunky white earbuds' ancestors.
Invented before the World Wide Web.DVD: DVDs came out in 1996, years after the Web was first launched in 1991.
Invented before the World Wide Web.MP3 player: Digital audio players arrived in the late 1990s, well after the Web.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Bluetooth: Named after Harald Bluetooth, a Danish king, and developed in the late 1990s, so after the Web.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi arrived in 1997, nearly a decade after the Web's invention.
Invented before the World Wide Web.USB: USB launched in 1996, years after the World Wide Web.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Google: Founded in 1998, almost a decade after the Web.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Blu-ray: Launched in 2006, by which point the Web was long established.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Emoji: Created in 1999 in Japan, after the Web.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Text message: The first SMS in December 1992 read 'Merry Christmas', a year after the Web went public.
Invented before the World Wide Web.Flash drive: Flash drives arrived around 2000 and quickly replaced floppy disks.
Invented before the World Wide Web.QR code: Denso Wave invented it in 1994 to track car parts, years after the Web's launch.

Internet protocols.HTTP: Hypertext Transfer Protocol, created by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN, is how your browser asks a server for a page.
Internet protocols.HTTPS: HTTP encrypted using TLS, which is why a padlock appears in your browser, and protects data in transit.
Internet protocols.FTP: File Transfer Protocol dates to the early 1970s and is one of the oldest internet protocols still in use.
Internet protocols.SMTP: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol moves email between servers, and dates from 1982.
Internet protocols.TCP: Transmission Control Protocol numbers packets and resends lost ones, so web pages and email arrive complete and in order.
Internet protocols.IP: The Internet Protocol handles addressing; IPv4 has only about 4.3 billion addresses, which led to IPv6.
Internet protocols.DNS: The Domain Name System works like the internet's phone book, translating names like example.com into numeric addresses.
Internet protocols.DHCP: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol quietly hands your phone an IP address when it joins a Wi-Fi network.
Internet protocols.SSH: Secure Shell lets you log in to remote computers over an encrypted connection, replacing the insecure Telnet.
Internet protocols.UDP: User Datagram Protocol skips delivery checks for speed, which suits video calls and online games.
Internet protocols.IMAP: Internet Message Access Protocol keeps email on the server, so all of your devices see the same inbox.
Internet protocols.POP3: Post Office Protocol version 3 downloads email to one device, an older approach compared with IMAP.
Internet protocols.HTML: HTML structures web pages with tags, but it's a markup language, not a protocol; HTTP delivers it.
Internet protocols.CSS: Cascading Style Sheets control how pages look, but it's a styling language, and not a protocol.
Internet protocols.JPEG: JPEG compresses photographs by discarding detail you barely notice, and it's a file format, not a protocol.
Internet protocols.USB: Universal Serial Bus is a physical connection standard for devices, not an internet protocol.
Internet protocols.SQL: Structured Query Language asks databases for data; it's a query language, not a network protocol.
Internet protocols.PDF: Adobe's Portable Document Format preserves layout on any device; it's a file format, not a protocol.
Internet protocols.RAM: Random access memory is your computer's short-term workspace, which is hardware and not a protocol.
Internet protocols.CPU: The central processing unit is the computer's main chip, hardware and not a network protocol.
Internet protocols.GIF: The Graphics Interchange Format from 1987 supports animation, but it's an image format, not a protocol.
Internet protocols.XML: Extensible Markup Language describes data with tags, but it's a format, not a network protocol.
Internet protocols.JSON: JavaScript Object Notation is the usual data format for web APIs, carried by protocols but not one itself.
Internet protocols.MP3: MP3 is an audio compression format that made digital music portable, not a protocol.

Characters in King Lear.King Lear: The aging king divides his kingdom among his daughters, a decision that brings madness and tragedy.
Characters in King Lear.Goneril: The eldest daughter flatters her father with big declarations of love, then quickly turns on him.
Characters in King Lear.Regan: The middle daughter is every bit as cruel as her sister and urges on the blinding of Gloucester.
Characters in King Lear.Cordelia: The youngest daughter refuses to flatter her father and loves him the most, but is banished.
Characters in King Lear.Edmund: Gloucester's illegitimate son schemes to take his brother's inheritance, declaring himself a proud bastard.
Characters in King Lear.Edgar: Gloucester's legitimate son flees and disguises himself as the madman Poor Tom.
Characters in King Lear.Gloucester: The earl whose eyes are put out on stage is one of the most shocking scenes in Shakespeare.
Characters in King Lear.Kent: The loyal earl is banished for speaking plainly to Lear, then returns in disguise to serve him.
Characters in King Lear.The Fool: The Fool is Lear's jester who speaks in riddles, and then vanishes from the play in the middle.
Characters in King Lear.Albany: Goneril's husband is the Duke of Albany, who turns against his wife after seeing her cruelty.
Characters in King Lear.Cornwall: The Duke of Cornwall is Regan's husband, and he is the one who puts out Gloucester's eyes.
Characters in King Lear.Oswald: Goneril's steward does her dirty work, and is killed by Edgar.
Characters in King Lear.Ophelia: Hamlet's doomed love interest drowns in her own tragedy, set in Denmark rather than Lear's Britain.
Characters in King Lear.Horatio: Hamlet's loyal friend survives to tell the story in the Danish tragedy, not in Lear's Britain.
Characters in King Lear.Iago: Othello's scheming ensign is one of Shakespeare's great villains, but he belongs to a different tragedy.
Characters in King Lear.Cassio: Othello's lieutenant, who loses his post after being tricked into drunkenness, is not in King Lear.
Characters in King Lear.Prospero: The magician duke of The Tempest rules a lonely island, far from Lear's kingdom.
Characters in King Lear.Bottom: The weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream who gets a donkey's head belongs to a comedy.
Characters in King Lear.Mercutio: Romeo's witty friend, who dies cursing both houses, comes from Romeo and Juliet.
Characters in King Lear.Brutus: A conspirator in Julius Caesar who stabs his friend for Rome's sake, not Lear's court.
Characters in King Lear.Cleopatra: The queen of Egypt in Antony and Cleopatra is a different tragedy's heroine, not Lear's daughter Cordelia.
Characters in King Lear.Hamlet: The Danish prince from the tragedy of Hamlet has nothing to do with Lear's Britain.
Characters in King Lear.Miranda: Prospero's daughter in The Tempest has grown up seeing almost no one except her father.
Characters in King Lear.Portia: The clever heroine of The Merchant of Venice argues the case in court disguised as a lawyer.

Characters in Julius Caesar.Julius Caesar: He's killed halfway through, yet the play bears his name, and his ghost returns to haunt Brutus before the battle of Philippi.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Brutus: Brutus is the real tragic hero, torn between love of Caesar and love of Rome. Caesar's last words are "Et tu, Brute?"
Characters in Julius Caesar.Cassius: Caesar says he has "a lean and hungry look" and lures Brutus into the plot, partly with forged letters.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Mark Antony: His "Friends, Romans, countrymen" speech turns the crowd against the conspirators, by repeating "Brutus is an honourable man".
Characters in Julius Caesar.Octavius: Caesar's heir, who becomes Augustus, Rome's first emperor, and with Antony defeats the conspirators at Philippi.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Calpurnia: Caesar's wife dreams of his murder and begs him to stay home on the Ides of March. He ignores her.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Portia: Brutus's wife, who in the play kills herself by swallowing hot coals, a detail Shakespeare took from Plutarch.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Casca: The conspirator who strikes the first blow, and who describes in Act 1 the crown being offered to Caesar three times.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Cinna: There are two in the play: a conspirator and a poet, and the mob tears the poet apart by mistake.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Lepidus: One of the three men who ruled Rome after Caesar, and Antony dismisses him as a man fit only to run errands.
Characters in Julius Caesar.The Soothsayer: He warns Caesar to "Beware the Ides of March", meaning March 15, and Caesar dismisses him as a dreamer.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Cicero: Rome's great orator appears briefly in the play, saying little. In real life he was killed on the triumvirs' orders in 43 BC.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Cleopatra: She's in Antony and Cleopatra, not this play, though Caesar's historical affair with her happened in his lifetime.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Coriolanus: Title hero of a different Roman play, set about 450 years before Caesar, in the early Republic.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Titus: Titus Andronicus is Shakespeare's bloodiest Roman play, set in a vague late Rome, a different story altogether.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Lavinia: Titus Andronicus's daughter, who suffers a brutal attack. She belongs to that gruesome play.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Tamora: Queen of the Goths in Titus Andronicus, who unknowingly eats a pie baked with her own sons.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Nero: A real Roman emperor, but he ruled a century after Caesar's death and Shakespeare doesn't put him on this stage.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Caligula: He reigned about eighty years after Caesar died, so he's far too late for this play, though he was Augustus's great-grandson.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Spartacus: Led his slave revolt in 73 BC, around the time Caesar was rising. He's famous from history and film, not Shakespeare.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Iago: Othello's scheming ensign. Like Cassius, he plants poison in a friend's ear, but he's from a different play.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Enobarbus: Antony's loyal officer in Antony and Cleopatra, known for the barge speech. He isn't in Julius Caesar.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Volumnia: Coriolanus's formidable mother, who talks her son out of attacking Rome. She belongs to the play named after him, not this one.
Characters in Julius Caesar.Hamlet: Polonius in Hamlet says he once played Julius Caesar at university and was killed by Brutus, but Hamlet is not in this play.

Elves in Tolkien's books.Legolas: The Mirkwood prince is the only elf in the Fellowship; his Sindarin name means "green leaf".
Elves in Tolkien's books.Elrond: He is half-elven and master of Rivendell; his twin brother Elros chose a mortal life as king of Númenor.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Galadriel: She was born in Valinor, saw the Two Trees shine, and remained in Middle-earth for thousands of years as Lothlórien's lady.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Arwen: She gives up her immortal life to marry Aragorn, and her choice is Tolkien's story of a love across lifespans.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Thranduil: In The Hobbit he isn't even named, just the Elvenking who imprisons Thorin's dwarves; Tolkien named him later.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Celeborn: Galadriel's husband and a lord of Lothlórien; his name means "silver tree" in Sindarin.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Glorfindel: The elf who rides out to rescue Frodo and the others; legend says he died battling a Balrog in Gondolin and was reborn.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Haldir: He's the March-warden of Lothlórien who greets the Fellowship; he dies at Helm's Deep in the films but not in the books.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Gil-galad: The last High King of the Noldor fell in battle with Sauron at the end of the Second Age.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Lúthien: She loves a mortal man, Beren, and Tolkien had her name carved on his wife Edith's gravestone.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Fëanor: The greatest craftsman among the Elves forged the Silmarils, and his Oath led to centuries of war.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Círdan: The Shipwright, one of the oldest elves, built the ships to Valinor and gave Gandalf the ring Narya.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Aragorn: He's a Dúnadan, a man descended from Númenor, who lives to be 210, but he isn't an elf.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Gimli: A dwarf, famous for his axe and friendship with Legolas.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Frodo: Hobbits are small people, not elves, and Frodo is one.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Gandalf: One of the wizards, an angelic Maia spirit in a human form, not an elf.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Dobby: Dobby is J. K. Rowling's house-elf, from Harry Potter, not from Tolkien.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Treebeard: An Ent, a tree-shepherd who is far older than any elf, and walks and talks.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Boromir: A man of Gondor, the Steward's son who dies protecting the hobbits, Merry and Pippin.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Faramir: Another man of Gondor, Boromir's younger brother, who marries Éowyn.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Éowyn: A woman of Rohan who slays the Witch-king, who was said no man could kill.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Bilbo: A hobbit and Frodo's uncle, who discovered the ring and wrote his own tale.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Gollum: Gollum was once Sméagol, a hobbit-like river creature, twisted by the ring.
Elves in Tolkien's books.Thorin: A dwarf king, grandson of Thrain, who leads the quest in The Hobbit.

Aviation terms.Aileron: Aileron is French for 'little wing', and these flaps on the trailing edge make an airplane roll.
Aviation terms.Fuselage: Fuselage comes from French for 'spindle-shaped', and it is the long body that holds crew, passengers and cargo.
Aviation terms.Taxiway: Taxiways are lettered, like Alpha and Bravo, and runways are numbered, so pilots can follow named routes on the ground.
Aviation terms.Hangar: A hangar shelters aircraft, and the word comes from Old French for an enclosure.
Aviation terms.Mayday: Mayday comes from the French 'm'aider', meaning 'help me', proposed in the 1920s by Croydon Airport radio officer Frederick Mockford.
Aviation terms.Turbulence: Turbulence rarely endangers a plane, since airliners are built to withstand much worse, but unbuckled passengers can be thrown about.
Aviation terms.Altitude: Pilots above a certain altitude set their altimeters to a standard pressure, so all planes share a common height reference.
Aviation terms.Runway: A runway's number is its compass heading divided by ten, so runway 27 points west.
Aviation terms.Jet lag: Jet lag is usually worse flying east, because it is easier for the body clock to stretch than shorten.
Aviation terms.Tailwind: Jet-stream tailwinds can make transatlantic flights east to west slower, and west to east faster, by an hour or more.
Aviation terms.Landing gear: Wright brothers' plane used skids and early planes used wheels, and modern gear is tucked away to cut drag.
Aviation terms.Fathom: A fathom is a six-foot measure of water depth, so it is a nautical unit.
Aviation terms.Bilge: The bilge is a ship's lowest part, where dirty water collects, so it isn't an aviation term.
Aviation terms.Gangplank: A gangplank is the board you walk onto a ship, so it belongs to boats.
Aviation terms.Caboose: A caboose is the crew car at the end of a freight train, so it belongs to railways.
Aviation terms.Sleeper: A sleeper is a railway tie or a bed on a night train, so it isn't aviation.
Aviation terms.Pantograph: A pantograph is the arm on an electric train that draws power from overhead lines.
Aviation terms.Hubcap: A hubcap covers a car's wheel center, so it is for cars, not planes.
Aviation terms.Odometer: An odometer counts a car's mileage, and planes use other instruments.
Aviation terms.Dipstick: A dipstick checks the oil in a car engine, so it is a car part.
Aviation terms.Siding: A siding is a short railway track, and it's not for airplanes.
Aviation terms.Crow's nest: The crow's nest is a ship's lookout platform high on the mast, and it's nautical.
Aviation terms.Mainsail: The mainsail is a sailing ship's biggest sail, so it is nautical.
Aviation terms.Kickstand: A kickstand props up a bike or motorbike, and planes have none.

Necklines.V-neck: The V shape draws the eye downward and is thought to make the neck look longer, which is why it flatters many people.
Necklines.Crew neck: Named after the sweaters worn by rowing crews, and still the standard cut for a plain T-shirt.
Necklines.Scoop neck: A wide, rounded U shape that dips lower than a crew neck, and a staple of summer tops.
Necklines.Turtleneck: Called a polo neck in Britain, this high rolled collar became the daily uniform of Steve Jobs.
Necklines.Halter: Named after the halter on a horse, with straps that go around the neck and leave the shoulders and back bare.
Necklines.Boat neck: In French it's called bateau, meaning boat, and Coco Chanel helped popularize it with her Breton sailor tops.
Necklines.Sweetheart: Shaped like the top of a heart, with a curved dip at the center and a soft line across the chest.
Necklines.Cowl neck: Cowl comes from Latin cuculla, a monk's hood, and the draped folds of fabric echo that hood.
Necklines.Off-the-shoulder: Made famous by Brigitte Bardot in the 1950s, which is why it is sometimes called the Bardot neckline.
Necklines.Square neck: A straight-across neckline common in Renaissance gowns, and still used for formal and vintage-style dresses.
Necklines.Mock neck: A short, high turtleneck that sits snug at the neck but is not folded over, a modern compromise between collar and neckline.
Necklines.Bootcut: A trap: bootcut is a jeans leg that flares slightly over boots, so it describes trousers, not a neckline.
Necklines.A-line: Christian Dior introduced the A-line silhouette in 1955; it describes a skirt shape, not a neckline.
Necklines.Raglan: Raglan is a sleeve, named after Lord Raglan, a British commander in the Crimean War who had lost an arm at Waterloo.
Necklines.Cap sleeve: A cap sleeve just covers the top of the shoulder, so it describes the sleeve, not the neckline.
Necklines.Bell sleeve: A bell sleeve flares out like a bell from the elbow, and it is a sleeve, not a neckline.
Necklines.Empire waist: The empire waist sits high, just under the bust, and was popularized by Empress Josephine in Napoleon's France.
Necklines.Pleated: Pleats are folded fabric, a texture of cloth, not the shape of a neckline.
Necklines.Pencil: A pencil skirt is a slim, narrow skirt that runs to the knee, so it belongs to a different part of the outfit.
Necklines.Flared: Flared describes legs or skirts that widen toward the hem, and it has nothing to do with a neckline.
Necklines.Peplum: A peplum is a short ruffle at the waist, from the Greek peplos, an ancient garment, so it describes a waistline.
Necklines.Skinny: Skinny is a snug jeans fit that went mainstream in the 2000s, not a neckline.
Necklines.Drop waist: The drop waist is a low waistline typical of 1920s flapper dresses, so it is not about the neck.
Necklines.Puff sleeve: A puff sleeve is gathered and rounded at the shoulder, popular in Elizabethan times, and it doesn't describe the neckline.

New Orleans Mardi Gras.Beads: Purple, green and gold beads are thrown from floats by the millions, and the colors stand for justice, faith and power.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.King cake: The plastic baby hidden inside is a tradition: whoever finds it is expected to buy the next cake or host the next party.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Masks: In New Orleans, riders on floats are legally required to wear masks, a rule meant to keep them anonymous.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Floats: Some floats at Mardi Gras World are built months ahead from foam and papier-mache; the biggest krewes run floats with dozens of riders.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Jester hat: The jester's cap in purple, green and gold is the carnival's unofficial symbol, tied to the fool who is allowed to mock the powerful.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Krewe: These private social clubs build and fund the parades; Rex, Zulu and Endymion are among the best known, and the name is a Mardi Gras-spelling of crew.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Doubloons: These aluminum or wooden coins are stamped with a krewe's emblem and thrown to the crowd; they are collected as souvenirs.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Bourbon Street: Famous for its bars and balconies, the street hosts a wild party all year but is mostly kept clear of the big parades, which take other routes.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Fat Tuesday: The French name Mardi Gras means this: the last day of feasting before Lent begins on Ash Wednesday.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Parade: Parades roll for about two weeks before the holiday, and Mardi Gras day itself is a legal holiday in Louisiana.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Pumpkin: Pumpkins belong to Halloween and autumn harvest, not to the carnival season that ends before Lent.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Turkey: Turkey is the centerpiece of American Thanksgiving, which falls in November, long after Mardi Gras.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Mistletoe: Kissing under mistletoe is a Christmas custom, with roots in Norse myth and Celtic druid lore, not carnival.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Menorah: This nine-branched candelabrum is lit at Hanukkah, a winter festival of lights unrelated to carnival.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Shamrock: Shamrocks are the emblem of St. Patrick's Day on March 17, a separate holiday from Mardi Gras.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Candy cane: Candy canes are a Christmas treat; the hook shape is often said to represent a shepherd's crook, though the story is debated.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Egg hunt: Egg hunts belong to Easter, which comes after Lent; Mardi Gras is the party that precedes the fasting.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Dreidel: Spun at Hanukkah, each side of this top bears a Hebrew letter that tells players to win or lose pot items.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Mooncake: Mooncakes are eaten at the Mid-Autumn Festival in September or October, with a salted egg yolk often hidden in the center.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Sugar skull: Decorated skulls of sugar belong to Mexico's Day of the Dead in early November, not New Orleans carnival.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Yule log: This chocolate log cake comes from the old Yule tradition of burning a log at midwinter, so it is a Christmas thing.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Maypole: Dancers weave ribbons around this tall pole on May Day, an old spring tradition across Europe.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Red envelope: Red envelopes with money are given at Lunar New Year and weddings, and red stands for luck in Chinese culture.
New Orleans Mardi Gras.Hot cross bun: Traditionally eaten on Good Friday, this spiced bun is marked with a cross and has a nursery rhyme about it.

Ways to tell fortunes.Tarot cards: Tarot began as a 15th-century Italian card game. Fortune-telling use came in the 18th century.
Ways to tell fortunes.Crystal ball: Used for scrying, staring into a sphere to see visions. Elizabethan scholar John Dee famously had one.
Ways to tell fortunes.Palm reading: Palmists read the heart, head and life lines, a practice found in India, China and ancient Greece.
Ways to tell fortunes.Tea leaves: Called tasseography. Leaves left in a cup after tea are read for symbols, a favorite parlor activity in Victorian Britain.
Ways to tell fortunes.Astrology: It started in Babylon, not in newspaper columns. It's different from astronomy, which studies the actual stars.
Ways to tell fortunes.Runes: Letters of ancient Germanic alphabets, called the futhark after its first six letters. Divination with them is mostly a modern revival.
Ways to tell fortunes.I Ching: The Chinese Book of Changes is about 3,000 years old. Tossing coins or yarrow stalks builds one of 64 hexagrams.
Ways to tell fortunes.Numerology: Assigns meaning to numbers from your name or birthdate. Tradition credits Pythagoras, who believed numbers ruled reality.
Ways to tell fortunes.Coffee grounds: Tasseomancy: after drinking Turkish coffee, the cup is turned onto its saucer and the patterns are read.
Ways to tell fortunes.Horoscopes: The word means "hour-watcher" in Greek. Newspaper sun-sign columns began in a British paper in 1930.
Ways to tell fortunes.Hypnosis: A medical or therapy tool, not fortune-telling. It's a trap because stage hypnotists appear to see your mind.
Ways to tell fortunes.Acupuncture: A Chinese medicine technique that inserts thin needles. It's about health, not predicting your future.
Ways to tell fortunes.Aromatherapy: Uses scented oils for mood and health claims. No prophecy involved, so it's not a way to tell fortunes.
Ways to tell fortunes.Reflexology: Pressing points on the feet and hands. Claims about it are popular, but it isn't a fortune-telling method.
Ways to tell fortunes.Meditation: A calming mental practice with roots in many religious traditions. It's about attention, not predicting your future.
Ways to tell fortunes.Yoga: Its Sanskrit name means "to yoke" or unite. It's an exercise and philosophy, not a method of prediction.
Ways to tell fortunes.Ventriloquism: A trap: ancient Greeks thought belly-voiced speaking was a prophet's gift. But today it's a stage act with puppets.
Ways to tell fortunes.Juggling: Depicted in an Egyptian tomb painting about 4,000 years old. It's a performance skill with no foretelling.
Ways to tell fortunes.Sleight of hand: A magician's skill, not a fortune teller's. Fortune tellers lean on cold reading, not quick fingers.
Ways to tell fortunes.Origami: Japanese paper folding. The children's paper fortune-teller is folded, but origami itself is just an art.
Ways to tell fortunes.Calligraphy: The art of beautiful writing. The Greek word means "beautiful writing," and it doesn't predict anything.
Ways to tell fortunes.Reiki: A Japanese energy-healing practice from the 1920s, developed by Mikao Usui. It's therapy, not prophecy.
Ways to tell fortunes.Karaoke: Japanese for "empty orchestra." It's a singing entertainment, though some use songs to lighten the future.
Ways to tell fortunes.Mime: Silent performance art. Marcel Marceau made it famous, and no mime has ever predicted anything.

Players in the Hanukkah story.Judah Maccabee: Led the Jewish revolt after his father's death and retook the Temple in 164 BCE; 'Maccabee' may mean 'hammer'.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Mattathias: A priest from Modi'in who sparked the revolt in 167 BCE by refusing to make a pagan sacrifice.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Antiochus: Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a Seleucid king who banned Jewish practices and defiled the Temple, was nicknamed 'Epimanes', or 'madman'.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Hasmoneans: The dynasty descended from the Maccabees ruled Judea for about a century.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Modi'in: The village where the revolt began; a modern Israeli city of the same name now stands nearby.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Seleucids: A Greek-ruled empire carved from Alexander's conquests, centered in Syria and Mesopotamia.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Hellenists: Jews who adopted Greek customs; the revolt was also a civil conflict among Jews.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Jerusalem: The Temple here was rededicated, and 'Hanukkah' itself means 'dedication'.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Eleazar: A Maccabee brother who died at Beth Zechariah when he charged under a war elephant.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Jonathan Maccabee: Judah's brother, who became high priest and leader after Judah fell in 160 BCE.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Nebuchadnezzar: Babylon's king who destroyed the First Temple in 586 BCE, centuries before Hanukkah.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Cyrus: The Persian king who let the Jews return and rebuild the Temple, long before the Maccabees.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Haman: The villain of the Purim story, a different holiday entirely.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Esther: The heroine of Purim in Persia, not of Hanukkah.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Ahasuerus: The Persian king in the Purim story, not in Hanukkah.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Pompey: The Roman general who captured Jerusalem in 63 BCE, about a century after Hanukkah.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Herod: Rebuilt and expanded the Second Temple from about 20 BCE, long after the Maccabean revolt.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Titus: Destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE, over two centuries after Hanukkah.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Masada: A mountain fortress where Jewish rebels held out against Rome in 73 CE; Herod had fortified it.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Pharaoh: The Passover story, much earlier than the Maccabees.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Vespasian: A Roman general who led the war in Judea in 67 CE before becoming emperor.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Mordecai: Esther's cousin in the Purim story, not Hanukkah.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Pontius Pilate: Roman prefect of Judea around 26 to 36 CE, two centuries after the Maccabees.
Players in the Hanukkah story.Julius Caesar: A Roman who lived in the first century BCE, after Hanukkah's events.
